passage:
Training coordinator's note, Wednesday, design studio.
At the eleven o'clock review, Dhruv flipped through Tejas's façade drawings for the school project in under a minute, said "Not good enough. Redo it," and moved to the next desk. No example, no mark on the sheets. Tejas said "Okay" very quietly. For the next hour I watched him open and close the same file, change a window size, change it back. At lunch he didn't eat. When I asked how it was going, he said, "I don't even know what's wrong. The windows? The colour? Me?" His voice cracked on the last word.
What I did: I asked Dhruv for three specific points before evening. Dhruv wrote them down: the entrance is hard to find, the sunshades face the wrong way, the front is too busy. I sat with Tejas while he read them. He nodded slowly. "I can fix those."

qa.q: How long did Dhruv spend on Tejas's drawings at the review?
qa.a: Under a minute.

qa.q: How was Tejas feeling after the review?
qa.a: He felt stung and lost, unsure what was wrong and even wondering if the problem was him; his voice cracked and he skipped lunch.

qa.q: What did the coordinator's step do that the review did not?
qa.a: Asking Dhruv for three specific points turned a hurtful verdict into things Tejas could act on: the entrance, the sunshades and the busy front.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have seen that one-minute review?
qa.a: Dhruv was probably rushing between desks and may have thought "not good enough" was clear, without noticing it told Tejas nothing and hurt a lot.

grounding: Shows a young worker given "not good enough" with no example, left both hurt and lost until specific points arrive.

subtype: Giving feedback that can be used [Response]
passage: The exhaust fan in the café kitchen in Shillong had died that morning, and service started in fifteen minutes. In the heat and clatter, Ganga held out a spoon of her new pumpkin soup, the first dish she had created for the menu. Devika tasted it and didn't make her wait. "The ginger and smoked chilli on top, that's the best thing in it. Keep that exactly." She tasted again. "The salt builds, though. By the last spoonful it's too much, because the stock is already salted. Go easy on the salt at the end. And the bread cubes go soft in two minutes, so serve them on the side." Ganga's shoulders came down from where they had been hunched. "Less salt at the end, bread on the side. Got it." She adjusted the pot while Devika checked the tandoor. By the first order, the soup went out with a little bowl of crisp cubes beside it.

qa.q: Why did Devika say the salt built up by the last spoonful?
qa.a: Because the stock is already salted.

qa.q: How was Ganga feeling while holding out the spoon, and how did that change?
qa.a: Ganga was nervous, shoulders hunched over her first menu dish, and then relieved once the comments came clear and kind.

qa.q: What made Devika's comments easy to act on?
qa.a: She named what worked, the ginger and chilli, pointed to two exact changes, the salt at the end and the bread on the side, and said why, all straight away.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had only said "too salty, fix it" in the rush?
qa.a: Ganga might have felt stung and guessed at the fix, perhaps losing the topping that worked, with no time before service to find out.

grounding: Illustrates a reviewer giving quick, specific, kind feedback that names what works, points to exact changes and explains why, so it is acted on at once.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage:
Friday
The LED circuit for the physics project finally lit up at 9:40 pm, and I have no idea why.
It wouldn't glow all evening. I panicked and started changing everything: flipped the LED, swapped the red and black wires, moved the resistor two holes down, borrowed Papa's new battery, pressed everything harder into the board. Somewhere in there it came on. I screamed and Papa came running.
Kamal, my lab partner, texted: "What was wrong?" I typed "fixed it!!" and then just sat there. Fixed WHAT? I changed about eight things at once and didn't write any of them down.
Now I'm scared to even touch it in case it goes off again before Monday's demo. Not really the feeling you want after "fixing" something. 😬
Mahima

qa.q: What time did the LED circuit finally light up?
qa.a: At 9:40 pm.

qa.q: How does Mahima feel after the circuit lights up?
qa.a: Mahima is relieved at first but then uneasy and scared, not knowing which change worked or whether it will fail before the demo.

qa.q: What could Mahima try next time the circuit won't work?
qa.a: Change one thing at a time, test after each change, and jot it down, so the fix is known and can be repeated at the demo.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel if the circuit fails again at Monday's demo?
qa.a: As lab partner, Kamal would likely be worried and let down after the cheerful "fixed it!!", with nothing to go on to fix it quickly.

grounding: Shows a teenager who panics over a faulty circuit, changes many things at random and cannot tell what fixed it, so nothing is learned.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
subtype: Blaming the tool or the world [Actor]
passage:
Wed, 11:15 pm
Spent three hours convinced the survey form was broken. The average age of my respondents came out as 94. Obviously the form was scrambling the data. I wrote an angry message to the course helpdesk and told Sunaina the university's tools are a joke.
Sunaina, very calmly: "Did you look at the raw answers?"
No. Why would I? I built the form myself, I know what's in it.
Except... row 38: someone typed their birth year, 1998, instead of their age. Row 71: "20 yrs". Two more birth years further down. The form was fine. My assumption that everyone would type a plain number was the broken part.
Deleted the helpdesk message before sending it. Mildly mortified.
Note to self: check what I assumed before blaming the machine.
Ankita

qa.q: What did row 38 contain instead of an age?
qa.a: A birth year, 1998.

qa.q: How does Ankita feel on finding the birth years?
qa.a: Ankita feels mildly mortified, embarrassed about the angry helpdesk message and the three hours spent blaming the form.

qa.q: What could Ankita do first the next time a result looks impossible?
qa.a: Look at the raw answers and list what was assumed, such as everyone typing a plain number, before deciding the tool is broken.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see the whole evening?
qa.a: Sunaina stays calm and maybe a little amused, seeing a simple check Ankita skipped, and helps with one question instead of arguing.

grounding: Shows a student who blames the tool for a wrong result before checking an unverified assumption, which turns out to be the real fault.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: At eleven at night in the Behala flat, Binita's sewing machine started skipping stitches, and Vandana's blouse had to be ready by morning for a cousin's haldi. Vandana had fallen asleep on the divan. Tired and alone with the whirr, Binita wanted to fiddle with everything at once. Instead she tore a strip of scrap cotton and sewed a test line. Every fifth or sixth stitch skipped. Good: she could make it happen on demand. On the back of an old electricity bill she wrote: 1. New needle. Sewed a strip. Still skipping. 2. Rethreaded the top. Still skipping. 3. Took out the bobbin case: a ball of lint inside. Cleaned it, sewed a strip. Clean line, fifty stitches, no gaps. She circled number 3, yawned, and went back to the blouse. At 1:20 she laid it, finished, beside Vandana's phone.

qa.q: What did Binita find inside the bobbin case?
qa.a: A ball of lint.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when the machine started skipping at eleven?
qa.a: Binita was tired and a bit lonely with Vandana asleep, and tempted to fiddle with everything at once in a rush.

qa.q: Why did writing each step on the bill help?
qa.a: Each change was tested alone and noted, so Binita didn't go round in circles while tired and knew exactly that the lint was the fault.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel waking up to the blouse beside the phone?
qa.a: Vandana would likely be relieved and grateful, perhaps without knowing how late Binita worked to fix the machine.

grounding: Illustrates making a fault repeat on demand, changing one thing at a time and writing down each result, which prevents circular guessing when tired.

passage:
Francis: nazia, 2 min? I've stared at this probability question for an hour
Nazia: go
Francis: bag with 5 red, 3 blue. pick 2 without putting back. P(at least one blue)
Francis: I did P(first blue) + P(second blue), then added P(both blue) because "at least one" includes both
Francis: which gives... wait
Francis: oh
Francis: OH. I'm counting the both-blue case twice
Francis: just do 1 minus P(no blue). 1 − (5/8 × 4/7) = 1 − 20/56 = 36/56
Nazia: I literally said nothing 😄
Francis: you said "go". that was enough
Nazia: happy to be your rubber duck anytime 🦆
Francis: going for a walk before the next one. brain is soup

qa.q: What answer did Francis finally get?
How does Francis feel when the mistake appears mid-message?
qa.a: Francis is suddenly relieved and a bit sheepish, after an hour of frustration, seeing the double-counting the moment it is spelled out.

qa.q: Why did typing the problem out to Nazia work?
qa.a: Explaining each step in order slowed Francis down and broke the tunnel vision, so the error showed up without Nazia saying anything.

qa.q: How does Nazia see the exchange?
qa.a: Nazia is amused and pleased to have helped just by listening, and offers to do it again.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: At 6:10 pm, rush hour, all eight ticket gates at the metro station stopped reading cards. Commuters bunched up behind the barriers, and the station master, two guards and Deepak from the control centre crowded into the equipment room behind Lavanya. Her heart was pounding so hard she could hear it. She opened the gate controller screen and her mind went white; the checklist she had practised a dozen times had simply vanished. "Restart everything," someone said. "Change the network cable," said someone else. Her hand hovered over three settings at once. Deepak leaned in and asked quietly, "What changed today?" She blinked. "The card-reader update. This morning." She rolled back that one update on one gate. It beeped green. Then the other seven, one by one. Afterwards, in the corridor, her hands were still shaking.

qa.q: How many ticket gates stopped reading cards?
qa.a: All eight ticket gates.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling as everyone crowded behind her?
qa.a: Lavanya was panicking: her heart pounded, her mind went white and the practised checklist vanished, while her hand hovered over several changes.

qa.q: What could help Lavanya think clearly the next time a failure happens with people watching?
qa.a: Keep a short written checklist taped by the screen, starting with "what changed today?", and try one change on one gate before touching the rest.

qa.q: How might Deepak have seen the moment?
qa.a: Deepak probably saw that Lavanya knew the answer but was flooded by pressure, and chose one quiet question instead of adding another theory.

grounding: Shows a young engineer facing a live failure with people watching, whose racing heart and narrowed thinking push her towards changing many things at once.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: "Honestly, I'm still thinking about Saturday. I'm Damini, I was on the media team for the convocation livestream. Ten minutes in, the online audience lost all sound. Parents abroad were typing NO AUDIO in the chat. Our lead was shouting that the internet had crashed, someone else swore the streaming site was down, and I was half convinced a virus had got in. Ira, the quiet one from IT, walked over to the desk and asked three boring questions. 'Can the hall hear the speaker?' Yes. 'Is the sound reaching the mixer? Look at the lights.' Yes, they were bouncing. 'Is it reaching the laptop?' The laptop's sound bar was flat. A cable had been kicked half out when someone moved a chair. Two minutes, fixed. No genius. Ira just refused to guess. I felt a bit silly about my virus theory, to be honest."

qa.q: What had happened to the cable?
qa.a: It had been kicked half out when someone moved a chair.

qa.q: How did Damini feel watching Ira fix it?
qa.a: Damini was impressed by Ira's calm and felt a bit silly about the virus theory.

qa.q: What can the media team learn from how Ira handled it?
qa.a: Follow the sound step by step from the hall to the mixer to the laptop with simple questions, instead of shouting theories.

qa.q: What might the crisis have been like for Ira?
qa.a: Ira seemed steady and focused, perhaps treating it as a simple chain to check, though from outside no one can be sure how calm Ira felt inside.

grounding: Shows colleagues noticing one calm person asking simple questions while others guess loudly, and that method, not brilliance, solves it.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: "Rashmi, you asked why I looked like a ghost on Sunday. I'm Hrithik, I look after maintenance at the hotel, and on Saturday the main lift stopped between the second and third floors during a wedding. Nobody was inside, thank god, but three hundred guests had to share one small lift. I was up in the machine room with a torch in my mouth, tracing the fault, and my phone rang every four minutes. Front office: 'Any update?' Banquets: 'The bride's family is asking.' The general manager: 'How long?' Every call, I lost my place in the wiring diagram and had to start the check again. After an hour I did something I'd never dared. I sent one message to all three: 'I'll post an update in the managers' group every twenty minutes. Please don't call unless someone is stuck.' The calls stopped. Forty minutes later I found the burnt relay."

qa.q: How often did Hrithik's phone ring during the search for the fault?
qa.a: Every four minutes.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel with the calls coming in?
qa.a: Hrithik felt frustrated and pulled in different directions, losing the place in the wiring diagram and restarting the check each time.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik's one message help?
qa.a: It gave the managers a single place and a set time for updates, so the calls stopped and Hrithik could work without interruption until the burnt relay turned up.

qa.q: How might the managers have seen their own calls?
qa.a: They were probably anxious themselves, with guests and the bride's family asking, and didn't realise each call was slowing the repair.

grounding: Shows a person fixing a fault while managers keep asking for updates, and how one update channel at a set interval protects the fixer's focus.

passage: "Ojas, you keep saying you'll pick your stream when you're sure. Let me, your Tarun chacha, tell you about my summer of waiting to be sure. I was sixteen. The choice was the polytechnic in Nashik for electrical, or commerce at the local college. I wanted a sign. I asked my teacher, then the astrologer uncle next door, then I waited for my board result to decide for me. It came, good marks, and still no sign. My friend Sandeep filled his form in May and kept saying, 'Just choose, you can change later.' I kept waiting. By the time I went to Nashik in July, electrical was full. I took mechanical, the only seat left, and spent two years with a knot in my stomach every morning. Not because the choice was wrong. Because I never actually made it."

qa.q: Which course did young Tarun end up taking?
qa.a: Mechanical, the only seat left.

qa.q: What was young Tarun feeling through that summer?
qa.a: He was anxious and unsure, wanting a clear sign before choosing, and later felt a knot in his stomach every morning.

qa.q: What could young Tarun have done in May, when Sandeep filled his form?
qa.a: He could have picked the option that seemed best so far and applied, knowing he could change later, instead of waiting for certainty.

qa.q: How might Sandeep have seen Tarun's waiting that summer?
qa.a: Sandeep was probably puzzled and a bit worried, seeing that waiting was costing more than a choice would, which is why he kept saying "just choose".

grounding: Shows a teenager who waits months for certainty about a course, and the waiting narrows his options and adds to his worry.
